questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to separate your rubbish for recycling at home
Why recycling isn't enough, and the circular economy
Which countries produce the most waste each year
How washing machines are made and then sold
questions.why: They hear that recycling is not the answer, and discuss the circular economy as a possible solution.

questions.q: Why does Sam say “that's a bit harsh” at the start?
options: Neil has criticised the way she does her recycling
Neil forgot her name when introducing the show
Neil says the topic of the programme is boring
She thinks Neil means they are talking nonsense
questions.why: When Neil says “we're talking rubbish”, Sam takes it as an insult, but he means the topic is rubbish.

questions.q: What does Sam do with her rubbish at home?
options: She separates it into paper, metal, food and plastic
She burns all of it in a corner of her garden
She takes it to a recycling centre every single day
She doesn't recycle at all because she's too busy
questions.why: She says she's always very careful to separate her rubbish into paper, metal, food, plastic and so on.

questions.q: According to Alexandre Lemille, why isn't recycling the answer?
options: It is far too expensive for most cities to run
People refuse to recycle, even when it's easy
Not all waste can be separated and treated properly
There are not enough bins in the streets and parks
questions.why: He says we can't get all the waste separated properly and therefore treated.

questions.q: What does Lemille say is the main aim of our current model?
options: To reduce waste
To hide waste so people don't see it
To sell waste to other countries
To turn waste into energy
questions.why: He says the main objective is to hide waste, so it is out of sight and out of mind.

questions.q: What does Sam admit about her own rubbish?
options: Once it's collected, she doesn't think about it
She knows exactly where it goes and what happens
She often forgets to put it out on the right day
She sends some of it to other countries herself
questions.why: She says her rubbish is collected and she doesn't really think about what happens to it after that.

questions.q: In a circular economy, who is responsible for a product's lifecycle?
options: The consumer who buys it
The local council
The shop that sells it
The manufacturer that makes it
questions.why: Manuela Saragosa says the manufacturer retains responsibility for the lifecycle of the product.

questions.q: What does Sam think would be a result of the circular economy?
options: Products would become much cheaper in the shops
People would buy more and more new products
Makers would try to make products last longer
Recycling would stop completely in most cities
questions.why: Sam says, “this would make manufacturers try to make their products last longer!”
